case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in PLRA cases, the Seventh Amendment requires a jury (rather than a judge) to resolve disputed facts about administrative-exhaustion when those facts are intertwined with the merits of the prisoner’s underlying claim.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Prison Litigation Reform Act (exhaustion requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a)) and the Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial in suits at common law.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that PLRA exhaustion is a threshold, judge-resolvable issue akin to other preconditions to suit, and that courts may hold evidentiary hearings and make factual findings on exhaustion without violating the Seventh Amendment—even if the exhaustion facts overlap with merits facts—because Congress designed the PLRA to screen and dismiss unexhausted claims early to reduce the burden of prisoner litigation on state and local governments.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that when exhaustion turns on genuinely disputed facts that are bound up with the merits (e.g., whether officials retaliated or thwarted access to the grievance process), having a judge decide those disputes usurps the jury’s constitutional function; thus, in such intertwined cases, the Seventh Amendment entitles the prisoner to a jury determination of the disputed facts (or at least forbids a judge from resolving them at a preliminary exhaustion hearing in a way that effectively decides the merits).
key_precedents: Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., 517 U.S. 370 (1996)
City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes at Monterey, Ltd., 526 U.S. 687 (1999)
Fidelity & Deposit Co. v. United States, 187 U.S. 315 (1902)
Fireman's Fund Insurance Co. v. Railway Express Agency, Inc., 253 F.2d 780 (6th Cir. 1958)
McPherson v. Mich. High Sch. Athletic Ass'n, Inc., 119 F.3d 453 (6th Cir. 1997)
Crane v. Ind. High Sch. Athletic Ass'n, 975 F.2d 1315 (7th Cir. 1992)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the strongest Seventh Amendment point: when “unavailability” depends on alleged intimidation or retaliation, the same credibility dispute may overlap with liability and a judge-first finding can, as a practical matter, end the case. But Beacon Theatres and Dairy Queen are chiefly concerned with judicial factfinding that precludes a later jury determination on legal claims; we can answer that concern by a narrow holding that permits judges to resolve contested facts solely for the § 1997e(a) gatekeeping question, while expressly denying any merits-preclusive effect and reserving liability and damages for the jury if the suit proceeds. Justice Alito’s and Justice Thomas’s emphasis on the PLRA’s text (“no action shall be brought”) and the tradition of judicial resolution of threshold defenses—consistent with Markman’s functional allocation—supports treating exhaustion as an antecedent condition to suit that courts must enforce early. On my minimalist approach, the correct path is to decide only who decides exhaustion/unavailability and to cabin the ruling so it cannot be used to erode the jury’s role on overlapping merits issues in later proceedings.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the most serious objection: that “unavailability” fact disputes can overlap with § 1983 merits and that judge-made credibility findings may, as a practical matter, decide the case. But under the Seventh Amendment’s original public meaning, the question is whether this statutorily created, antecedent condition on bringing suit—§ 1997e(a)’s command that “[n]o action shall be brought” absent exhaustion—was historically allocated to a jury; it was not, and Congress’s text makes it a gatekeeping determination courts must enforce. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed cabining—judicial findings limited strictly to exhaustion and expressly non-preclusive on merits—answers Beacon Theatres/Dairy Queen’s concern because the judge is not adjudicating liability or damages, only whether the action may proceed at all. Fidelity & Deposit and Galloway confirm that judicial resolution of preliminary matters involving factual determinations does not “diminish the substance” of the jury right when, if the statutory precondition is satisfied, the merits remain for a jury.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s core objection—that “unavailability” fact disputes can overlap with merits and thus a judge’s credibility determinations effectively decide liability—does not overcome the PLRA’s textual command that “[n]o action shall be brought” absent exhaustion, which frames the issue as an antecedent condition on suit rather than an element of a § 1983 claim. As the Chief Justice notes, Beacon Theatres/Dairy Queen are principally concerned with judge-first determinations that preclude later jury resolution of legal claims; we can and should cabin exhaustion factfinding to the gatekeeping question and make clear it carries no merits-preclusive effect if the case proceeds. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Fidelity & Deposit and Galloway reinforces that judicial factfinding on preliminary matters is consistent with the Seventh Amendment when it does not displace the jury on liability and damages. Requiring a jury whenever a prisoner pleads intimidation would, as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, convert Congress’s early screening mechanism into routine merits-style jury litigation and substantially frustrate the PLRA’s practical operation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s administrability proposal—judge factfinding on exhaustion, expressly nonpreclusive on the merits—does not solve the Seventh Amendment problem identified in Beacon Theatres/Dairy Queen, because the constitutional injury is functional displacement of the jury by a judge-first credibility determination on the same coercion/retaliation facts that define liability in a § 1983 action. Even if formally “cabined,” an adverse judicial finding on intimidation or thwarting typically ends the case at the gate, so the jury never decides those historically legal, damages-linked facts, which is precisely the practical diminishment Beacon Theatres warned against. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Galloway and Fidelity & Deposit does not undermine this: those cases bless judicial sufficiency devices within the jury-trial framework, not reassignment of overlapping, merits-determinative historical fact disputes to a judge by labeling them “threshold.” The workable line remains to permit judges to resolve genuinely separable, procedural exhaustion disputes, but require jury resolution (or deferral to trial) when “unavailability” turns on contested official misconduct intertwined with the merits, to protect access to justice for incarcerated plaintiffs and preserve the substance of the jury right.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the hardest Seventh Amendment point: when “unavailability” rests on retaliation or obstruction, the exhaustion hearing can mirror the merits and a judge’s credibility call can effectively end the case. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Beacon Theatres/Dairy Queen are principally about judge-first factfinding that binds or precludes the jury on legal claims; we can adopt a rule that the court’s findings are strictly for the PLRA’s “no action shall be brought” gatekeeping determination and have no merits-preclusive effect if the suit proceeds. Markman’s history-plus-workability framework supports assigning this system-managing, antecedent eligibility question to judges where there’s no clear 1791 jury analogue and where a jury-first requirement would regularly convert § 1997e(a) into a merits-like trial just to decide the gateway. That cabining—paired with careful sequencing and explicit nonpreclusion—answers the functional concern without undermining the statute’s coherent operation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press a serious Seventh Amendment concern: that when “unavailability” depends on alleged retaliation or obstruction, a judge’s credibility determinations may overlap with merits and effectively end the case. But the PLRA’s text—“[n]o action shall be brought” absent exhaustion—creates an antecedent statutory condition on access to federal court, and under Markman’s allocation framework (as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize) we may assign such threshold, system-administering determinations to the judge where history offers no clear jury analogue and where doing so preserves Congress’s design. Beacon Theatres/Dairy Queen’s functional worry is addressed by the narrowing approach Chief Justice Roberts proposes: judicial factfinding is limited to the exhaustion gate and expressly carries no merits-preclusive effect, leaving liability and damages for the jury if the action may proceed. Requiring a jury whenever a prisoner alleges thwarting would, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, convert a statutory prerequisite into routine merits trials without a demonstrated 1791 requirement, and that is not how I read the Seventh Amendment’s original meaning.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is the functional Beacon Theatres/Dairy Queen concern that an “unavailability” hearing can mirror the merits and, practically, decide the case through credibility findings. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, the constitutional problem in that line of cases is judge-first factfinding that binds or precludes the jury on legal claims; we can avoid that by expressly cabining exhaustion findings to the PLRA’s statutory gatekeeping inquiry and giving them no merits-preclusive effect if the suit proceeds. The PLRA’s text (“no action shall be brought”) and Markman-style workability considerations, emphasized by Justice Kagan, reinforce that Congress designed exhaustion to be an early screen administered by judges, and requiring juries whenever thwarting is alleged would convert the threshold into a de facto merits trial and undermine that structure. Galloway and Fidelity & Deposit, as Justice Thomas notes, support the broader principle that judicial resolution of preliminary access-to-court conditions—without adjudicating liability or damages—does not diminish the Seventh Amendment’s substance.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson fairly identify the hard case: “unavailability” can hinge on alleged retaliation or obstruction that also bears on § 1983 liability, so a judge’s credibility findings may feel merits-like. But the PLRA’s text—“[n]o action shall be brought … until such administrative remedies as are available are exhausted”—casts exhaustion as an antecedent statutory condition on maintaining the action, and under Markman’s allocation logic (as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize) the absence of a clear 1791 jury analogue plus workability concerns supports judicial resolution of that gateway even when factfinding is required. Beacon Theatres/Dairy Queen’s Seventh Amendment worry is principally about depriving a later jury through preclusion or practical displacement; adopting Chief Justice Roberts’s cabining rule—findings limited to exhaustion and expressly non-preclusive on merits—answers that constitutional concern while preserving Congress’s screening design. City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes underscores the jury’s primacy on ultimate liability and damages, but it does not compel a jury trial for every disputed predicate fact where the court is determining only whether the statutory prerequisite to suit has been met.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s cabining proposal (no merits-preclusive effect) addresses formal issue preclusion, but it does not answer the Beacon Theatres/Dairy Queen functional concern that a judge’s credibility finding on the same alleged retaliation/thwarting facts can, in practical consequence, end a legal damages case and displace the jury’s historic role. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Markman’s workability allocation is powerful for administrability, yet Markman involved an interpretive, judge-suited issue; here the exhaustion “unavailability” inquiry can require live credibility determinations about official misconduct that are indistinguishable from core § 1983 merits facts. Justice Thomas’s Fidelity & Deposit and Galloway points confirm judges may resolve some preliminaries, but those precedents do not justify reallocating overlapping, liability-determinative historical facts to a judge simply by labeling them “threshold.” I would therefore preserve judicial resolution for genuinely separable exhaustion disputes, but require jury resolution (or deferral to trial) when exhaustion turns on genuinely disputed, merits-bound facts about defendants’ misconduct that would otherwise be tried to a jury.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1997e(a) makes exhaustion a mandatory precondition to suit, and consistent with longstanding practice courts may resolve threshold defenses through evidentiary hearings and factual findings without converting every predicate dispute into a jury question. The Seventh Amendment inquiry asks whether judge factfinding here would diminish the “substance of the common-law right of trial by jury,” and it does not where the exhaustion determination functions as a gatekeeping issue and any overlap facts can still be tried to a jury on the merits if the case proceeds. Beacon Theatres/Dairy Queen concerns preserving the jury right when an equitable determination would effectively preclude a later jury trial, but exhaustion findings need not have preclusive effect on the merits, avoiding that constitutional problem while honoring Congress’s PLRA design to screen unexhausted claims early. A narrow rule allowing judges to decide disputed exhaustion facts—while making clear that merits issues remain for the jury—best respects precedent, federalism interests in prison administration, and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Seventh Amendment preserves the jury right as it existed at common law, but it does not forbid courts from using post-1791 procedural mechanisms that keep non-merits, gatekeeping issues with the judge, even when factual development is required. Congress in the PLRA made exhaustion mandatory—“[n]o action shall be brought” absent exhaustion, 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a)—which functions as a threshold bar to suit that courts may and should resolve at the outset to limit federal-court intrusion into state prison administration. This Court has held that judicial resolution of certain threshold matters (including via summary judgment and directed verdict) does not violate the Seventh Amendment, see Fidelity & Deposit Co. v. United States, 187 U.S. 315, 319–21 (1902), and Galloway v. United States, 319 U.S. 372, 388–93 (1943). So long as the judge’s factfinding is confined to exhaustion and does not purport to enter a merits judgment beyond that statutory precondition, the Constitution does not require submitting those exhaustion disputes to a jury.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The PLRA’s exhaustion mandate, 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a), establishes a threshold precondition to suit that Congress intended courts to enforce early to screen out unexhausted claims and reduce the burdens of prisoner litigation on government defendants. The Seventh Amendment preserves the jury trial right as it existed at common law, but it does not prohibit judges from resolving preliminary, gatekeeping issues—even when that requires factfinding—much as courts routinely do for other pretrial matters. Beacon Theatres and Dairy Queen articulate a prudential sequencing principle aimed at preventing an equitable determination from foreclosing a later jury trial via preclusion; an exhaustion ruling does not function that way because it determines only whether the case may proceed in federal court, not the ultimate liability, and applying a jury requirement here would substantially frustrate the PLRA’s design and practical operation. Consistent with this Court’s functional approach to allocating judge/jury roles in mixed questions, see Markman v. Westview Instruments, the better reading is that exhaustion fact disputes are for the judge.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The PLRA’s exhaustion requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a), is a mandatory precondition, but it cannot be administered in a way that strips prisoners of the Seventh Amendment jury right when the disputed “exhaustion” facts are bound up with the very merits of a § 1983 claim—such as whether officials intimidated, retaliated, or otherwise thwarted access to the grievance process. Under Markman v. Westview Instruments and City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes, the Seventh Amendment preserves the jury’s historic role over factual questions in actions analogous to those tried at law in 1791, and courts must not reallocate merits-determinative factfinding to judges by relabeling it “threshold.” A judge may resolve purely procedural, separable exhaustion disputes, but where the factual dispute effectively decides liability-related facts, the Constitution requires the jury to resolve them (or the case to proceed with those facts tried to the jury). This approach respects Congress’s screening aims while ensuring fairness and access to justice for vulnerable incarcerated litigants whose claims often hinge on contested credibility and coercion.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1997e(a) makes exhaustion a mandatory precondition to suit, and Congress designed that requirement to operate as an early, threshold screen—so courts must be able to resolve exhaustion before reaching the merits. Under this Court’s Seventh Amendment framework, we look to historical practice and functional considerations in allocating judge-versus-jury decisionmaking, and Markman v. Westview Instruments supports treating certain preliminary, system-managing determinations as for the judge where that allocation is more workable and coherent with the statutory scheme. Even when exhaustion-related facts overlap with merits facts (e.g., whether officials thwarted the grievance process), a judge’s finding on the threshold exhaustion question need not usurp the jury’s role on liability so long as it does not bind merits factfinding beyond the exhaustion determination. Requiring juries to decide exhaustion whenever there is factual overlap would undermine the PLRA’s structure and administrability by converting a gatekeeping prerequisite into routine jury-triable merits litigation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The PLRA’s text makes exhaustion a mandatory precondition to suit—“[n]o action shall be brought” until remedies are exhausted, 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a)—and that kind of threshold eligibility to proceed is appropriately resolved by the court as a matter of judicial gatekeeping. Under the Seventh Amendment’s historical inquiry, we ask whether the issue is of a sort tried to a jury in 1791 and whether allocating it to the judge preserves the “substance” of the jury right; Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc. instructs that some issue-allocation to judges is consistent with the Amendment even in actions at law. Exhaustion lacks a clear common-law jury analogue and instead resembles judge-resolved, forum/access-to-court doctrines; allowing a judge to find facts on exhaustion does not finally determine liability on the merits, and any merits issues in a properly exhausted case remain for a jury. Where overlap creates concern, ordinary tools (e.g., limiting findings to exhaustion and avoiding merits preclusion) can protect the jury’s role without constitutionalizing a jury trial on exhaustion.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1997e(a) of the PLRA makes exhaustion a mandatory precondition to suit, and Congress designed that requirement to operate as a threshold screen that courts can apply early to avoid unnecessary merits litigation. Under the Seventh Amendment’s history-and-tradition inquiry, this Court asks whether the specific issue must be submitted to a jury to preserve the 1791 common-law jury right; Markman v. Westview Instruments instructs that both historical practice and functional/workability considerations inform that allocation, and threshold, judge-resolved determinations are consistent with that framework. Allowing prisoners to obtain jury trials whenever they allege that officials thwarted grievances would be impractical and would undermine the PLRA’s structure by converting a gatekeeping requirement into a merits trial driver. The better course, consistent with judicial restraint and administrable procedure, is to permit judges to resolve disputed exhaustion facts at an evidentiary hearing even when some overlap with merits exists, while leaving the ultimate merits (if exhaustion is satisfied) for the jury.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The PLRA’s text makes exhaustion a mandatory precondition to bringing an “action” in federal court—“[n]o action shall be brought” until administrative remedies are exhausted, 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a)—which supports treating exhaustion as a threshold judicial determination rather than part of the merits submitted to the jury. Under the Seventh Amendment’s historical-analog framework, even where the underlying claim is legal in nature, the allocation question turns on whether the specific issue must be tried to a jury to preserve the 1791 common-law right; Markman instructs that courts may assign certain antecedent determinations to judges where history and functional considerations support judicial administration. Allowing judges to resolve exhaustion fact disputes (including overlapping facts) at an evidentiary hearing best fits Congress’s screening design in § 1997e(a) and avoids converting a statutory precondition into a merits jury question. This approach remains consistent with Seventh Amendment doctrine permitting judicial resolution of preliminary matters without usurping the jury’s role on ultimate liability and damages once the case properly proceeds to trial.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The PLRA’s exhaustion mandate, 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a), is a threshold requirement, but when its resolution turns on genuinely disputed facts that are intertwined with the merits—such as whether officials’ retaliation or obstruction rendered remedies “unavailable”—a judge’s credibility-based factfinding at a preliminary hearing risks effectively deciding the core liability dispute that the Seventh Amendment reserves to a jury. Under Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., the Court looks to history and functional considerations to preserve “the right to a jury’s resolution of the ultimate dispute,” and City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes confirms that where history is unclear, functional concerns about the jury’s role matter. Pragmatically and in service of procedural fairness, courts can still treat exhaustion as a gatekeeping issue, but must avoid resolving overlapping, merits-bound factual disputes in a way that predetermines the jury’s verdict; those disputes should be submitted to the jury (or postponed until trial) when they are inseparable from the merits.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in PLRA-governed prisoner civil-rights suits, the Seventh Amendment requires a jury (rather than a judge) to resolve disputed facts about administrative exhaustion when those facts overlap with the merits of the prisoner’s claim.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Prison Litigation Reform Act (PLRA) exhaustion requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a), and the Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial in suits at common law.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that PLRA exhaustion is a threshold, judge-decided precondition to suit (an affirmative defense/abatement-type issue) and that courts may hold evidentiary hearings and make factual findings on exhaustion even when the facts are disputed, because doing so implements Congress’s goal of screening and efficiently disposing of unexhausted prisoner litigation; petitioner and amici emphasize that requiring jury trials on exhaustion would undermine PLRA efficiency, increase costs for state/local jail and prison operators, and turn a gatekeeping inquiry into merits litigation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that when disputed exhaustion facts are intertwined with (and effectively decide) the underlying merits—e.g., whether officials thwarted access to the grievance system or retaliated—the Seventh Amendment prohibits a judge from resolving those factual disputes at a preliminary stage; instead, a jury must decide the contested facts (or at minimum those that are merits-overlapping), because judicial factfinding on exhaustion can function like an impermissible merits determination that strips the prisoner of the constitutional right to have a jury resolve core factual disputes in a § 1983 action seeking legal relief.
key_precedents: Fidelity & Deposit Co. v. United States, 187 U.S. 315 (1902)
Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., 517 U.S. 370 (1996)
City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes at Monterey, Ltd., 526 U.S. 687 (1999)
Fireman's Fund Insurance Co. v. Railway Express Agency, Inc., 253 F.2d 780 (6th Cir. 1958)
McPherson v. Mich. High Sch. Athletic Ass'n, Inc., 119 F.3d 453 (6th Cir. 1997)
Crane v. Ind. High Sch. Athletic Ass'n, 975 F.2d 1315 (7th Cir. 1992)
Lee v. Willey (referenced by the lower court as authority for an evidentiary hearing procedure on exhaustion)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Ross “availability” disputes may require credibility findings about threats or retaliation and thereby risk becoming a de facto merits trial inconsistent with Del Monte Dunes’ preservation of the jury’s role in § 1983 damages actions. But as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 1997e(a)’s “no action shall be brought … until” frames exhaustion as an abatement-like condition precedent that courts historically enforced with necessary factfinding, and Markman’s history-and-function approach supports allocating that gatekeeping inquiry to the judge. Justice Kagan’s separability/intertwinement rule is appealing as a narrowing principle, yet I agree with Justice Barrett that it is too indeterminate and would invite relabeling and expanded discovery that undermines the PLRA’s screening function. The proper accommodation is to allow judicial factfinding only on what is necessary to exhaustion/availability while cautioning against (and avoiding issue-preclusive spillover from) merits-adjacent determinations, leaving any ultimate § 1983 liability facts for the jury if the suit proceeds.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Ross “availability” often turns on credibility about threats or retaliation and can look like the very § 1983 narrative the Seventh Amendment preserves for a jury under Del Monte Dunes. But the Constitution’s original public meaning preserves the jury right for “Suits at common law” on the merits once an action is properly before the court; it does not prevent Congress from imposing a textual condition precedent to suit, and § 1997e(a)’s command that “[n]o action shall be brought … until” exhaustion occurs is precisely such a threshold bar. As the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Markman’s history-and-function framework and the historical treatment of pleas in abatement support judge resolution of this gateway issue even when factfinding (including credibility) is required, so long as the court confines findings to what is necessary to exhaustion/availability and does not purport to adjudicate ultimate liability. Justice Kagan’s separability/intertwinement proposal is not grounded in a stable historical line and would, in practice, invite recharacterization of merits facts to defeat the PLRA’s prerequisite rather than enforce its text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: Ross “availability” can hinge on credibility about threats or obstruction, and a judge’s resolution may feel like a merits mini-trial implicating Del Monte Dunes. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 1997e(a)’s text (“[n]o action shall be brought … until”) makes exhaustion an antecedent condition to the suit itself—historically akin to a plea in abatement—so the Seventh Amendment jury right on § 1983 liability does not attach until that prerequisite is satisfied. Fidelity & Deposit and Galloway do not establish a constitutional bar on judicial factfinding for threshold statutory preconditions; they address sufficiency devices within an action properly before the jury, not whether Congress may require courts to determine a gateway bar before the action may proceed. The proper safeguard, consistent with Roberts’s proposal, is to cabin judicial findings strictly to what is necessary to decide exhaustion/availability and to avoid any preclusive merits determination beyond that narrow gatekeeping function.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s best point is the abatement-like text of § 1997e(a) (“no action shall be brought … until”) and Markman’s history-and-function framework, which can justify judge resolution of genuinely threshold, procedural prerequisites. But their proposed constraint—judges finding only what is “necessary” to exhaustion/availability—does not meaningfully protect the Seventh Amendment where Ross v. Blake makes “availability” turn on credibility-laden allegations of threats, retaliation, or deliberate thwarting by the very officials sued; deciding those facts is not a detachable gatekeeping inquiry but a merits-adjacent narrative a jury traditionally resolves in a § 1983 damages action, as City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes emphasizes. Fidelity & Deposit and Galloway underscore that judges may remove issues from juries only through legal-sufficiency mechanisms, not by creating a parallel bench factfinding track that routinely decides disputed credibility and intent under the banner of “exhaustion.” I therefore agree with Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson that, at minimum, when “availability” depends on contested misconduct facts intertwined with liability, the Constitution requires those facts be resolved by a jury (or via Rule 56/JMOL standards), not by a judge at an evidentiary hearing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability objection is the strongest point for Petitioners: a rule that any overlap triggers a jury could hollow out § 1997e(a)’s “no action shall be brought … until” gatekeeping. But Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s proposed limiter—judge finds only facts “necessary” to exhaustion—does not solve the Seventh Amendment problem in Ross “availability” cases where the necessary facts are credibility-laden allegations of threats/obstruction by the very officials sued; deciding those facts is not meaningfully distinguishable from deciding the core § 1983 narrative a jury traditionally resolves, as Justice Sotomayor stresses and Del Monte Dunes illustrates. Markman’s history-and-function framework supports judge resolution for genuinely separable, procedural/documentary exhaustion disputes, yet it supplies no stable historical warrant for reallocating disputed, merits-adjacent historical facts to the judge simply because Congress labeled exhaustion a precondition. I therefore remain with a middle path: courts may decide exhaustion when the dispute is procedural and separable, but when “availability” turns on contested misconduct facts that would effectively function as a merits finding, the Seventh Amendment requires jury resolution of those facts.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: Ross “availability” can require credibility findings about threats or obstruction that resemble the merits narrative, risking a de facto merits trial without a jury. But under § 1997e(a)’s text (“[n]o action shall be brought … until”), exhaustion is a precondition to suit, and Markman’s history-and-function framework supports assigning abatement-like threshold determinations to judges even when factfinding is required. Chief Justice Roberts’s limiting principle is therefore essential and, in my view, sufficient under our originalist Seventh Amendment analysis: the court may find only those facts necessary to decide exhaustion/availability and must avoid adjudicating ultimate § 1983 liability or giving preclusive effect to merits-adjacent determinations beyond the gateway. Justice Kagan’s separable/intertwined test, though appealing, lacks a stable historical anchor and would predictably invite strategic pleading and discovery to force jury resolution of what Congress made a threshold bar.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: Ross “availability” can require credibility findings about threats or obstruction that resemble the merits, raising a real Del Monte Dunes concern about juries in § 1983 damages suits. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch correctly ground the allocation in § 1997e(a)’s “no action shall be brought … until” text and the Markman history-and-function approach: courts historically resolved threshold bars to suit (abatement-style) even when factbound, and the Seventh Amendment jury right attaches to the merits once the statutory gateway is cleared. Fidelity & Deposit and Galloway do not undermine that framework because they address sufficiency devices within an action, not Congress’s ability to impose and courts’ duty to enforce a precondition to bringing any action at all. The workable safeguard is Roberts’s: judicial factfinding must be confined to exhaustion/availability and should not be given preclusive effect on ultimate liability facts, preserving the jury’s role if the PLRA threshold is satisfied.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: in some Ross “availability” disputes, deciding whether officials threatened or thwarted grievances can look like deciding the core § 1983 story, raising a serious Del Monte Dunes Seventh Amendment concern. But § 1997e(a)’s text—“[n]o action shall be brought … until”—creates a precondition to suit that, as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, resembles a plea in abatement that courts historically resolved, even with limited factfinding, under Markman’s history-and-function approach. The constitutional answer is not Justice Kagan’s “intertwined/separable” jury trigger (too indeterminate and lacking a clear historical hook), but a cabined judicial inquiry: findings strictly necessary to exhaustion/availability, with no merits adjudication or issue-preclusive spillover into liability questions reserved for the jury if the case proceeds. Fidelity & Deposit and Galloway do not compel a different allocation because they concern sufficiency devices within a properly commenced action, whereas exhaustion is a statutory condition precedent to bringing the action at all.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s best point is the PLRA’s abatement-like text (“no action shall be brought … until”) and Markman’s history-and-function framing, which support judicial resolution of many threshold prerequisites even when some factfinding is required. But that does not answer the Seventh Amendment allocation where Ross “availability” turns on disputed, credibility-laden allegations of intimidation or deliberate obstruction that are functionally the same narrative facts a jury would decide on § 1983 damages liability under City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes. Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Barrett’s proposed limiter—judicial findings confined to what is “necessary” for exhaustion—fails as a practical constraint in these cases because the very “necessary” finding (e.g., whether officers threatened or retaliated to deter grievances) can effectively decide the core wrongdoing story without a jury. Fidelity & Deposit and Galloway reinforce, as Justice Sotomayor notes, that courts may remove issues from the jury only via legal-sufficiency mechanisms, not by creating a parallel bench credibility trial on merits-intertwined facts that the Seventh Amendment preserves for juries in actions at law.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1997e(a) makes exhaustion a mandatory precondition to suit, and longstanding practice permits judges to resolve threshold, non-merits prerequisites—including by evidentiary hearing—without violating the Seventh Amendment, so long as the court is not adjudicating ultimate liability. Under Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., we look to history and functional considerations in allocating decisionmaking, and the PLRA’s gatekeeping purpose would be substantially undermined if exhaustion disputes routinely required juries. Galloway v. United States and Fidelity & Deposit Co. v. United States confirm that the Seventh Amendment does not forbid judicial resolution mechanisms that prevent cases from reaching a jury where the law requires a preliminary showing. A narrow rule is appropriate: judges may find facts necessary to decide exhaustion under § 1997e(a), while avoiding merits determinations beyond what exhaustion requires and preserving the jury’s role on the underlying § 1983 claim.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Seventh Amendment preserves the jury-trial right as it existed at the Founding in “Suits at common law,” but it does not forbid Congress from imposing a statutory precondition to suit like the PLRA’s mandatory exhaustion requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a), and assigning its administration to the court. Exhaustion functions as a threshold, abatement-like issue concerning whether the action may proceed at all, and judges historically resolved such preliminary matters without a jury; nothing in the Seventh Amendment’s text requires a jury to decide disputed facts bearing on that gatekeeping inquiry. City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes confirms that a § 1983 claim for legal relief is triable to a jury on the merits, but it does not constitutionalize jury resolution of every antecedent statutory condition that determines whether the merits may be reached. Consistent with this Court’s recognition that judicial resolution of pretrial issues can be compatible with the Seventh Amendment (e.g., Fidelity & Deposit Co. and Galloway), a judge may find facts necessary to enforce § 1997e(a) even if they overlap with merits-related allegations.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1997e(a) makes exhaustion a mandatory precondition to suit, and the PLRA’s text and evident purpose are to screen out unexhausted claims early; that gatekeeping function would be substantially undermined if any overlapping factual dispute automatically required a jury trial. The Seventh Amendment preserves the substance of the 1791 jury right, but it does not bar courts from having judges resolve threshold, non-merits prerequisites to proceeding—especially where Congress has imposed a strict “no action shall be brought” limitation. Markman confirms that judge-jury allocation turns on history and functional considerations, and the functional consequences here strongly favor judge factfinding to avoid converting exhaustion into full-blown merits litigation. Unlike the directed-verdict and summary-judgment cases (Galloway; Fidelity & Deposit), the procedure here does not authorize merits adjudication without a jury; it determines only whether the lawsuit may proceed in light of § 1997e(a).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A § 1983 suit seeking legal relief is an action at law, and the Seventh Amendment preserves the jury’s role in resolving genuine disputes of fact central to liability. City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes confirms the jury-trial right on the merits in § 1983 actions, and Ross v. Bernhard instructs that we look to the nature of the particular issue—here, disputed “exhaustion” facts that overlap with whether officials thwarted or retaliated against the prisoner, effectively deciding the merits. While 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a) makes exhaustion mandatory, it does not authorize a judge to conduct a preliminary evidentiary hearing that resolves merits-overlapping factual disputes, which is distinct from the permissible use of summary judgment or directed verdict where no genuine fact dispute exists (Fidelity & Deposit; Galloway). Preserving a jury determination on intertwined facts best protects access to justice for vulnerable prisoners and prevents exhaustion from becoming a merits shortcut that strips the constitutional right to a jury trial.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1997e(a) makes exhaustion a mandatory precondition to suit, but it does not clearly assign to judges the power to resolve, at a preliminary evidentiary hearing, disputed facts that are also elements of (or defenses to) a legal § 1983 claim. In a suit seeking legal relief, the Seventh Amendment preserves the jury’s role over historically jury-triable factual questions; § 1983 is treated as analogous to an action at law, and the Court has emphasized that the allocation turns on the nature of the issue, not the stage of the litigation. See City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes, 526 U.S. 687, 709, 718 (1999); Markman v. Westview Instruments, 517 U.S. 370, 376 (1996). Workably, courts may still have judges decide exhaustion when it is genuinely separable (e.g., purely documentary timing/filing disputes), but when the exhaustion dispute is intertwined with merits facts (such as official thwarting or retaliation), the Seventh Amendment requires those disputed facts be resolved by a jury rather than judicial factfinding that effectively decides the claim.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The PLRA provides that “[n]o action shall be brought” until “such administrative remedies as are available are exhausted,” 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a), establishing a threshold precondition to suit that Congress meant courts to enforce before reaching the merits. The Seventh Amendment preserves the jury trial right as it existed in 1791, but exhaustion (including the Ross v. Blake inquiry into “availability”) is a gatekeeping issue akin to traditional pleas in abatement and equitable-type defenses historically resolved by judges, not juries. Consistent with Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., courts may assign certain fact-laden determinations to judges where functional considerations and historical practice place the issue with the court, and resolving exhaustion first respects separation-of-powers limits by adhering to Congress’s screening command rather than expanding jury trial entitlement beyond its original scope. Ross v. Blake reinforces that “availability” is a legal limit on the exhaustion mandate; judges may therefore resolve contested availability facts at the threshold without converting the proceeding into a merits trial.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1997e(a) makes exhaustion a mandatory precondition to suit, and this Court’s PLRA cases (e.g., Woodford v. Ngo; Ross v. Blake) emphasize strict, workably administered exhaustion rules that screen unexhausted claims early. Consistent with longstanding practice that judges resolve threshold, non-merits gateway issues—including resolving predicate fact disputes—judicial factfinding on exhaustion fits within the Seventh Amendment framework recognized in Markman, which looks to history and functional considerations in allocating decisionmaking between judge and jury. Requiring a jury whenever “unavailability” facts overlap with merits allegations would undermine the PLRA’s efficiency and gatekeeping design and create an unworkable rule inviting merits discovery and trial on a preliminary defense. The better course is to allow district judges to hold evidentiary hearings and make exhaustion findings, while ensuring they do not finally adjudicate merits beyond what is necessary to decide § 1997e(a).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Seventh Amendment preserves the jury right as it existed in 1791, but it does not constitutionalize a jury determination for every fact dispute that arises before trial; it permits courts to allocate certain threshold determinations to judges consistent with historical practice and functional considerations. The PLRA’s text makes exhaustion a mandatory precondition to bringing an action (“No action shall be brought … until”), 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a), and that structure supports treating exhaustion as an antecedent, judge-resolved gatekeeping issue even if some facts bear on merits-adjacent conduct. Under Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., the Court looks to history and the judge/jury division to preserve the substance of the jury right, and nothing in that analysis requires converting a statutory precondition into a jury question simply because some evidence overlaps with the merits. Consistent with precedent allowing judicial factfinding on preliminary matters (and with Congress’s evident screening purpose in § 1997e(a)), a judge may hold an evidentiary hearing and resolve disputed exhaustion facts without violating the Seventh Amendment, leaving the merits of the § 1983 claim for the jury if the suit proceeds.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The PLRA’s exhaustion requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a), is a mandatory precondition, but it cannot be administered in a way that effectively resolves the merits of a § 1983 claim through judicial factfinding where legal relief is sought. Under the Seventh Amendment, the jury right turns on “the nature of the issue,” and § 1983 actions are paradigmatic suits at law with a preserved jury-trial right on disputed facts central to liability. City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes confirms that § 1983 legal claims ordinarily carry a jury entitlement, and Markman’s history-and-function inquiry cautions against reallocating to judges factual determinations that are traditionally for juries. As a matter of procedural fairness and practical consequence, when exhaustion disputes hinge on merits-overlapping facts (e.g., whether officials thwarted or retaliated to block grievances), those disputed facts must be resolved by a jury (or at least reserved for the merits jury), rather than by a preliminary evidentiary hearing that operates as a de facto merits adjudication.
